questions.stem: A finance analyst wants Claude in the company's Enterprise workspace to read budget files in a cloud drive. The drive connector does not appear, because the organization's owners have not enabled it yet. A colleague suggests a free browser extension that copies drive files into any chat window automatically. What should the analyst do to stay within the organization's AI policy while still getting the analysis done?

options.text: Install the extension for this one project, since the files stay inside the approved Claude workspace once they arrive
Connect the drive from a personal Claude account instead, where the connector is already available and set up
Ask the workspace owners to review and enable the connector, and upload the needed files manually in the meantime
Ask Claude in the company workspace whether the extension is safe, and use it if Claude finds no security concerns

questions.explanation: The missing connector is a decision by the workspace's owners, not a technical obstacle to route around: as the scenario states, connector availability in the company workspace is controlled at the organizational level. Requesting a review uses the proper channel, and uploading just the needed files into the already-approved workspace keeps the work moving without introducing an unvetted tool that touches company data.

whyWrong.A: The extension is itself an unapproved tool that gains access to company files. Where the data ends up does not make an unvetted data path acceptable under an approved-tools policy.
whyWrong.B: Moving company data to a personal account breaks the approved-tools boundary, whatever features that account happens to have.
whyWrong.D: Claude cannot approve software for your organization. Tool vetting belongs to the owners and the security team, not to the model's opinion.

questions.mindset: A disabled feature is a decision to respect and request, not a gap to work around.

questions.stem: A consultancy's AI policy says every client deliverable that Claude helped draft must include a short AI-assistance statement. A project manager tells a consultant to leave the statement off a market report because 'this client won't care, and it makes us look less expert.' The report is due tomorrow. What is the MOST appropriate action for the consultant?

options.text: Include the statement as the policy requires, and raise any disagreement with the policy owner rather than skipping it
Leave the statement off this time, because the project manager owns the client relationship and accepts the risk
Rewrite enough of Claude's draft by hand that the report no longer counts as AI-assisted, then omit the statement
Ask the client informally whether they mind AI involvement, and include the statement only if they say they do

questions.explanation: Disclosure rules exist so that the organization is consistently transparent, not so individuals can judge case by case whether a client would mind. A manager's preference does not override written policy. If the manager thinks the rule is wrong for this situation, the right route is the **policy owner**, who can grant an exception or change the rule.

whyWrong.B: Owning the client relationship does not give a manager authority to waive company policy. Exceptions come from the policy owner.
whyWrong.C: Rewording to escape the definition is a deliberate workaround. The policy covers work Claude helped draft, and it did.
whyWrong.D: The policy sets the rule, not an informal client poll. It also makes disclosure depend on who asks, which defeats its purpose.

questions.mindset: Seniority or convenience never turns a policy requirement into an option.

questions.stem: A charity's AI policy, written two years ago, bans uploading any spreadsheet to Claude. A volunteer coordinator wants Claude to tidy a spreadsheet of public event dates and venue names taken from the charity's own website. The task looks harmless, and the rule seems outdated. Which approach BEST fits good governance practice?

options.text: Upload the spreadsheet anyway, because the rule was clearly meant for personal data and this file contains only public information
Paste the cells into the chat as plain text, because the policy only names spreadsheet uploads and says nothing about text
Ask Claude to read the policy and confirm that this rule does not apply to public data before the upload
Follow the rule for now and suggest to the policy owner that it be updated to allow public data, explaining this use case

questions.explanation: Even when a rule looks outdated, individuals should not decide on their own that it no longer applies. The constructive move is to **comply and propose a change through the policy owner**, using the real use case as evidence. That improves the policy for everyone instead of creating quiet, inconsistent exceptions.

whyWrong.A: Deciding for yourself what a rule was 'really meant for' is unilateral reinterpretation. The owner should make that call.
whyWrong.B: Changing the format to slip past the wording keeps to the letter of the rule while breaking its intent. That is a workaround, not compliance.
whyWrong.C: Claude cannot interpret your organization's policy with authority. Its answer would not make the upload compliant.

questions.mindset: Fix a bad rule through its owner. Don't fix it by ignoring it.

questions.stem: An employee's company AI policy requires the final version of any AI-assisted customer analysis to be saved to the team's document system. The employee plans to run the analysis in an incognito chat, reasoning that because incognito chats are not saved to history, the work falls outside the policy's record-keeping rules. Which statement BEST corrects this reasoning?

options.text: The reasoning holds: a record-keeping rule can only apply to chats that the product actually saves, so incognito work is out of scope
Chat mode does not change the policy's scope: the final AI-assisted analysis must still be saved to the document system
Ask Claude at the start of the incognito chat not to retain or reuse the customer data, which satisfies the policy's intent
Switch memory off before starting, since the policy applies only to analyses whose details Claude can remember in later conversations

questions.explanation: A policy's scope is defined by the work it covers — here, AI-assisted customer analysis — not by which chat mode was used. Incognito may keep a conversation out of saved history, but the obligation to save the final version to the document system is unchanged. Asking the model not to retain data is not a policy control: the exam guide's own sample rationale states that instructing the model not to retain data does not satisfy the policy requirement.

whyWrong.A: The policy covers the analysis, not the chat storage. Whether or not the conversation is saved, the final AI-assisted analysis must go into the document system.
whyWrong.C: A request to the model changes nothing about what the policy requires. It is not a control, and it does not create the required record.
whyWrong.D: Memory settings do not define the policy's trigger. The trigger is the nature of the work, not whether Claude can remember it later.

questions.mindset: Chat modes change what the product stores. They never change what your policy requires.

questions.stem: A procurement officer's team policy says the reviewed, final version of any AI-assisted supplier evaluation must be stored in the procurement system, with a note that Claude assisted. The officer has been leaving final evaluations only in their Claude chat history, where they can find them easily. What should they do?

options.text: Nothing further, because the chat history already holds a complete, timestamped record of the evaluation work
Turn on memory so Claude keeps a lasting record of each evaluation that teammates can ask about later
Put the evaluations in a shared Project so the whole procurement team can open the conversations
Save each reviewed evaluation to the procurement system with the AI-assistance note the policy requires

questions.explanation: Record-keeping rules point to a **system of record** for good reasons: other people can find the record, it outlives any one person's account, and it is governed by the organization's retention and audit processes. A personal chat history does none of that reliably. The fix is simply to follow the rule as written, including the assistance note.

whyWrong.A: Chat history is tied to one user's account and is not the designated record. The policy names a specific system.
whyWrong.B: Memory is personal context for future chats. It is not a shared, auditable record, and the policy names a specific system of record.
whyWrong.C: A shared Project improves access, but it is still not the system of record the policy requires, and it skips the assistance note.

questions.mindset: The record belongs where the organization keeps records, not where it is convenient for you.

questions.stem: A company's AI policy requires legal review of any public statement drafted with Claude before release. Late on a Friday, a vice-president asks a communications officer to publish a Claude-drafted press statement about a product recall within the hour. The VP says, 'Skip legal, I take responsibility.' Which response is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Publish the statement, because a vice-president has the authority to accept the risk on the company's behalf
Ask Claude to check the statement for legal problems and publish it if Claude finds no issues worth flagging
Explain that the policy requires legal review, and contact legal's urgent or on-call route to get a fast review
Refuse to work on the statement at all until Monday, when the full legal team is back in the office

questions.explanation: Urgency and seniority are the classic pressures that tempt people to skip controls. A recall statement is exactly the kind of high-stakes public text the review rule exists for. The best answer **keeps the control and speeds it up**: hold the line on review and use an urgent route. That respects both the policy and the business deadline.

whyWrong.A: Unless the policy names the VP as someone who can waive review, a verbal 'I take responsibility' does not change the rule.
whyWrong.B: Claude's self-check is not the legal review the policy requires. A model cannot stand in for a named human control.
whyWrong.D: Over-correcting harms the business. The goal is a compliant fast path, not a delay until Monday.

questions.mindset: Under deadline pressure, accelerate the control. Don't remove it.

questions.stem: A team lead is rolling out Claude to 15 customer-success staff. The company's AI policy sets rules on which data may be shared, requires a standard AI-assistance line in certain customer documents, and names the compliance team as policy owner. Which TWO actions would MOST effectively help the team follow the policy consistently? Choose TWO.

options.text: Set up a shared Project whose instructions include the required assistance line and whose knowledge holds only approved materials
Ask each person to begin every chat by telling Claude to follow company policy, so the model enforces the rules
Have Claude summarize the policy, and circulate the summary as the team's official reference in place of the original
Brief the team on the key rules and on how to reach the compliance team when something is unclear
Let each person choose the Claude plan that suits them best, so nobody is slowed down by workspace limits

questions.explanation: Consistency at scale comes from **making the compliant path the default** and **making it easy to ask**. A shared Project with the right instructions and approved knowledge builds the rules into everyday use (Projects are configured exactly this way: instructions plus curated knowledge sources). A briefing that names the policy owner means people escalate unclear cases instead of guessing.

whyWrong.B: Telling the model to 'follow policy' is not a control. Claude does not know the company's policy unless it is given the policy, and it cannot enforce rules on users.
whyWrong.C: A summary can help orientation, but replacing the official policy with an AI paraphrase makes Claude's interpretation the authority. That is wrong, and it may drift from the real text.
whyWrong.E: Mixed personal plans break the approved-workspace rule and spread company data across accounts the organization does not govern.

questions.mindset: Make the compliant path the easy path, and make the policy owner easy to reach.

questions.stem: During a screen share, a data analyst notices that a teammate is pasting internal sales forecasts into a personal Claude Pro account. The company policy allows Claude only through the company workspace and asks staff to report suspected policy breaches to the security team. The teammate is a friend and says, 'It's just numbers, no names.' What should the analyst do?

options.text: Remind the teammate of the policy and follow the reporting process it sets, so the security team can judge what action is needed
Say nothing this time, because the forecasts contain no personal data and no real harm to the business has been done
Tell the teammate to delete those chats right away, which removes the risk without anyone else in the company needing to be involved
Advise the teammate to turn off the personal account's data-usage settings for model training, which completely settles the data issue

questions.explanation: The breach is about the **approved-tools rule**, not only about personal data. Internal forecasts are company data, and a personal account is outside the organization's governance. The policy asks staff to report, and security decides how serious it is and what to do. Raising it directly with the teammate is good, but it does not replace the reporting the policy requires.

whyWrong.B: 'No names' and 'no real harm' do not make it compliant. The policy restricts which tools may hold company data, not just personal data.
whyWrong.C: Deleting quietly hides a possible incident from the colleagues responsible for assessing it, and the data has already left the governed workspace.
whyWrong.D: Consumer data-usage settings do not make a personal account an approved tool for company data, and they cannot undo sharing that already happened.

questions.mindset: The rule covers the tool as well as the data. Report through the channel and let its owners judge the impact.

questions.stem: A support team has built a Claude Project that drafts replies to customer complaints, and their tests with made-up complaints look good. They plan to start using it with real customers next week. Their company's AI policy says any new use where AI-assisted content reaches customers needs approval from the AI governance group. They have not asked for it yet. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Run a small live pilot with a few customers first, so there is real evidence to show the governance group afterwards
Submit the use case for governance approval before going live, and continue internal testing with sample data meanwhile
Add a line to each reply saying it may contain AI-generated errors, which addresses the governance concern without delay
Treat the Project as already approved, because the company workspace it runs in was reviewed and approved by governance

questions.explanation: The policy ties approval to the **use case**, not just the tool. Reaching real customers is exactly the point where approval is required. The team can keep improving the Project with sample data while the review happens, so they lose little time and stay compliant.

whyWrong.A: A live pilot with real customers is going live. Gathering evidence by breaking the rule defeats the purpose of the approval step.
whyWrong.C: A disclaimer does not replace the approval step, and it is no substitute for review of a customer-facing use.
whyWrong.D: Approving a workspace does not approve every use inside it. The policy explicitly requires review for new customer-facing uses.

questions.mindset: Approval attaches to the use case, not only the tool.

questions.stem: A marketing team's own AI guideline says employees may upload customer survey comments to Claude. The company-wide AI policy, owned by the privacy office, says customer free-text data may be used only after the privacy office has reviewed the purpose. A marketer notices the two documents disagree and has a campaign analysis due soon. What should the marketer do?

options.text: Follow the team guideline, because it was written specifically for marketing work and is more relevant to the task
Upload the comments but strip the customer names first, which satisfies both documents at the same time
Follow the stricter company-wide rule, and flag the conflict to the privacy office and the team guideline's author
Ask Claude to compare both documents and follow whichever rule it judges to be the more recent and authoritative one

questions.explanation: When a local guideline conflicts with an organization-wide policy, the safe default is the **stricter, higher-level rule**. Flagging the conflict to both owners gets it fixed for everyone. The company-wide policy requires a purpose review by the privacy office, and removing names does not meet that requirement.

whyWrong.A: A team guideline cannot loosen a company-wide policy. Being more specific does not give it more authority.
whyWrong.B: Removing names is good practice, but the company policy requires a privacy-office review of the purpose. De-identifying does not satisfy that step.
whyWrong.D: Which policy governs is a question for the policy owners, not for the model's reading of two documents.

questions.mindset: When rules conflict, follow the stricter one and get the owners to settle it.

questions.stem: A billing coordinator used Claude to draft a customer email explaining a refund, and sent it after a quick read. The next day they realize the email promised a refund window twice as long as the company actually offers. The AI policy says errors in AI-assisted content that reaches customers must be reported to the operations risk team. Which TWO actions should the coordinator take? Choose TWO.

options.text: Delete the Claude conversation that contains the incorrect draft, so it cannot be found and reused by mistake later
Report the error promptly to the operations risk team, as the policy requires for AI-assisted content that reached a customer
Ask Claude why it made the mistake, and file the model's explanation as the root cause in the incident record
Add a standard disclaimer line to all future customer emails stating that message details may contain AI-generated errors
Keep the conversation and the sent email so the risk team can see what happened, and follow their guidance on correcting it

questions.explanation: Incident handling has two parts: **tell the right owner quickly** and **preserve the evidence** so they can assess impact and decide on the correction, for example a follow-up to the customer. The coordinator owns the error, because they sent the email after only a quick read; confident-sounding output must still be verified before it reaches customers.

whyWrong.A: Deleting the conversation destroys evidence the risk team may need, and quietly removing the draft looks like covering up the incident.
whyWrong.C: Claude's explanation of its own error is not a reliable root cause to file in the incident record. The process gap, sending after only a quick read, is part of the cause too.
whyWrong.D: A blanket disclaimer moves risk onto customers and does not stop wrong promises. Proper review before sending does that.

questions.mindset: Report fast, keep the evidence, and own the error. Never hide it.

questions.stem: An operations manager who uses Claude through the company's chat workspace wants Claude to watch the service-desk queue and automatically reassign ticket priorities in the ticketing system overnight. Nobody would review the changes. Under the company's AI policy, new integrations that let AI take actions in business systems need security and governance sign-off. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: Route the request to the governance owners and to the integration developers or architects, explaining the business need
Write a very detailed prompt that tells Claude exactly how to set priorities, so the automation will be safe to run
Try it on a personal account with a trial connector first, to prove the idea works before involving anyone else
Ask Claude to reassign priorities overnight but only for low-impact tickets, which keeps the risk small enough to skip sign-off

questions.explanation: An unattended system that **acts on a business system** is both a governance decision and a technical build. At the Associate level, the right move is to describe the need clearly and **route it to the right owners**: security and governance approve it, and Developers or Architects design it with proper controls. The certification explicitly expects Associates to recognize limits and escalate more technical work.

whyWrong.B: A better prompt does not provide the approvals, access controls or monitoring that an action-taking integration needs.
whyWrong.C: Testing with company data through an unapproved personal setup breaks policy before any approval exists.
whyWrong.D: The policy has no low-impact exemption. Narrowing the scope yourself does not replace the required sign-off.

questions.mindset: Know where your role stops. Route builds and approvals to their owners.

questions.stem: A project coordinator's company has enabled a project-tracker connector, but the owners have limited it so that Claude can read tasks and cannot create or change them. The coordinator wants Claude to update 40 task statuses after a planning meeting. The coordinator's personal account has the same connector with full write access. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Use the personal account just for the status updates, since the task data already lives in the tracker the company approved
Ask Claude in the company workspace to try the updates anyway, since the restriction may not apply to status fields
Copy the tracker data into a spreadsheet and have a personal-account chat produce an import file to load back in
Have Claude draft the status changes in the company workspace, apply them yourself, and ask the owners about write access

questions.explanation: The read-only limit is the workspace owners' deliberate configuration — an organizational decision about what Claude may do in a connected system, and not something to route around. Claude can still do the useful part: drafting the 40 status updates from the meeting notes. A human applies them, and a request goes to the owners if write access would genuinely be worth having.

whyWrong.A: Using a personal account to get around an organizational restriction is the textbook workaround the approved-tools rule forbids.
whyWrong.B: Deliberately probing a restriction is still trying to bypass it. Treat the setting as the owners' decision.
whyWrong.C: This routes company data through an unapproved account and looks for a side door around the read-only control.

questions.mindset: Admin restrictions are policy decisions. Let Claude help inside them, and request changes through the owners.

questions.stem: A content writer used Claude to draft a blog article about workplace wellbeing. The company's AI policy requires that published AI-assisted content (1) is reviewed by an editor before publishing and (2) carries the company's standard AI-assistance note. Which TWO steps satisfy the policy? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to double-check its own facts and citations, and treat that self-check as the editorial review
Add a generic note saying the article 'may contain errors' in place of the company's standard wording
Send the draft to an editor for a full review, and publish only after the editor signs it off
Include the company's standard AI-assistance note in the article, worded exactly as the policy sets it out
Rewrite the opening and closing paragraphs yourself so the finished article counts as human-written rather than AI-assisted

questions.explanation: The policy names two controls, and the answer is simply to **do both as written**: an editor reviews the article, and the article carries the standard note. Neither control can be replaced by a model step or a reworded disclaimer.

whyWrong.A: A model checking its own output is not the human editorial review the policy names.
whyWrong.B: A generic error disclaimer is not the required assistance note, and it reads as a liability shield rather than transparency.
whyWrong.E: Light edits do not change the fact that Claude helped draft the article. This is a workaround to avoid disclosure.

questions.mindset: When the policy names the controls, apply them exactly. Don't substitute look-alikes.

questions.stem: A research team at a health insurer wants Claude to help analyze claims data that includes members' diagnoses. The company's AI policy bans regulated health data from Claude unless the compliance office grants a documented exception. Their director gave verbal approval in a meeting, and the analysis is due in three weeks. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Submit a written exception request to the compliance office that explains the purpose, the data involved and the safeguards proposed
Proceed now with the full data, since the director's verbal approval in the meeting counts as an exception for the team
Split the claims data into small batches across several chats, so no single conversation holds a large amount of regulated data
Run the analysis from a personal API account outside the company workspace, because the ban applies only to the company's own Claude environment
Meanwhile, build and test the analysis approach with data that compliance confirms is permitted, such as synthetic or properly de-identified records

questions.explanation: The policy names **who grants exceptions (compliance) and how (documented)**. A director's verbal OK meets neither condition. The constructive path is to file a proper request and, in parallel, prepare the workflow with data compliance has confirmed is allowed — the same principle as the exam guide's guidance to redact or anonymize regulated identifiers so the work can proceed compliantly. If the exception is granted, the team is ready; if not, it still has a compliant approach.

whyWrong.B: Verbal approval from someone who is not the named exception owner is not a documented exception.
whyWrong.C: Splitting regulated data into smaller pieces still shares it. The ban applies to the data, not to batch size.
whyWrong.D: The policy bans regulated health data from Claude without a documented exception; it does not limit the ban to one workspace, and a personal account sits entirely outside organizational governance.

questions.mindset: Exceptions come from the named owner, in writing. Prepare compliantly while you wait.
